extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism and young newspaper reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria for gathering, selecting, structuring, and styling news and feature stories for daily newspapers; includes classification of newspaper contents, news values, sourcing, structure (leads/body), literary and typographical style, and an outline for analyzing examples. Intended as a classroom textbook/handbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of newspaper contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The contents of a typical daily paper may be grouped in seven classes: (1) news stories; (2) special feature articles; (3) editorials; (4) dramatic, musical, and literary criticism; (5) practical advice and useful information; (6) humorous matter; (7) fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of these, news stories, special feature articles, editorials, and criticism are the distinctly journalistic types. Use this classification to identify the function and expected treatment of each piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a news story
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories present (1) timely events of interest and significance to readers, and (2) timely incidents of little or no news value made entertaining by presentation (human interest or feature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'spot news' (events when they occur) from 'detail' or 'situation' material presented later as special correspondence or feature articles. Only timely events of significance warrant publication as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special feature article criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Special feature articles are detailed presentations of (1) matters of recent news warranting elaboration, (2) timely topics not directly connected with the news of the day, or (3) subjects of interest neither timely nor connected with current events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are informative, generally longer, often appear in magazine sections, and require development beyond the summary lead appropriate to pure news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of editorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials have as their purpose the interpretation of news and current issues and the discussion of matters of general interest with a view to convincing readers of a proposition and persuading action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorials differ from news and features by their argumentative, persuasive intention and evaluation of facts rather than simple reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local versus telegraph (general) news organization
rubrics_metrics.description: News gathering is divided into: (1) local news — gathered by reporters under the city editor or local bureau heads; (2) telegraph news — all non-local news arriving by telegraph, telephone, cable or mail from correspondents or associations (Associated Press, United Press).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the different chains of responsibility: newspaper correspondents answer to telegraph/state editors; press-association reporters answer to their association's division head. Use appropriate sourcing and editing workflows for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: How news is written under deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters write rapidly, sometimes at the scene, sending copy by messenger or telephone; when necessary a reporter may telephone facts to a rewrite man who writes the story. All copy is edited before print and may be substantially reworked by rewrite men, editors, or copy-readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fast writing does not excuse slovenly English. Expect editing; well-written copy may remain unchanged, poor copy can be remade. Use clear notes and full facts to facilitate rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions affecting news writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure and style of news stories are determined by (1) conditions under which written, (2) character of readers, (3) conditions under which newspapers are read, (4) typographical form of newspapers, and (5) popular taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for haste, audience education level, narrow column widths, rapid reading habits, and demand for novelty when choosing structure and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of news writing
rubrics_metrics.description: News writing must be (1) concise, (2) clear, (3) comparatively simple, (4) easily read, and (5) attractive to all classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance conciseness with attractiveness; simplicity aids rapid reading and broad appeal. Aim for these five as primary quality criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Conciseness requires omission of needless words, including only details necessary for effective presentation, and making story length proportionate to importance of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise writing need not be bald—retain style and interest while 'boiling down' copy. 'Cut it to the bone' is a newsroom maxim; always question each word's necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness (simplicity of diction and construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearness is secured by comparative simplicity of diction, sentence construction, and paragraph structure. Learned diction, elaborate figures, and involved sentences have no place in newspaper writing for broad readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer common words, straightforward syntax, and clear paragraphing. Explain technical terms when unavoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement for rapid reading (prominence by initial position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Important details are placed at the beginning of paragraphs and sentences to catch the eye in rapid reading; this produces a loose rather than a periodic sentence structure and eliminates the possibility of climactic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the key facts; use initial positions for emphasis. Structure body paragraphs to present most significant points early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph and line-length constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrow newspaper columns necessitate shorter paragraphs; a typical newspaper paragraph contains 36 to 76 words (versus 150–250 in ordinary prose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep paragraphs short and readable; avoid long blocks that appear heavy in columnar type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (and danger) of fiction devices in feature writing
rubrics_metrics.description: To make some news stories entertaining, newspapers sometimes abandon the conventional summary lead and use device like short-story openings; use of fiction techniques is commendable for effect but dangerous when fiction supplants factual accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fictional devices only to portray actual events faithfully; never invent details to heighten effect. Distinguish clearly between factual reporting and narrative techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of news stories (informative vs feature/human interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two general types: (1) informative news stories — chiefly to give facts (purely informative or constructive/influential), and (2) feature/human interest stories — chiefly to take material of little or no news value and make it interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informative stories usually have summary leads and prioritize facts; constructive informative stories aim to produce a wholesome effect and may vary length accordingly. Feature stories rely on literary skill to sustain reader interest and may avoid summary leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values (what makes something news)
rubrics_metrics.description: News values are based largely on reader interest in: (1) timely matters; (2) extraordinary events; (3) struggles for supremacy (politics, business, sports); (4) matters involving property, life, welfare of people; (5) children; (6) animals; (7) hobbies and amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of interest depends on familiarity with persons/places/things involved, their importance/prominence, and closeness of relation to reader's personal affairs. Use these as selection criteria and to judge space allotment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs general interest and 'local ends'
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction grows from greater interest in people and places known to the reader; interest varies inversely with distance from news origin. Telegraph/general news is given local interest by bringing out local ends (how it affects the community).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing or editing wire copy, emphasize local angles to increase reader relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sources include public and private records, reports, officials, and eye-witnesses; from story details it is often possible to infer sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note and compile sources used in examples to build a personal list for future reporting. Cite authorities where appropriate to support facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of news gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Details of how information was obtained can be inferred from stories (e.g., reporter's questions in interviews); gathering methods include on-scene reporting, interviews, telephone dispatches, telegraph, and correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze sample stories for implicit hints on methods; record practical techniques and adapt them to your beats. In urgent cases, feed facts to a rewrite man clearly and concisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and ethical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Every news story should present details as accurately and completely as significance warrants; embellishment, fictitious details, distortion or suppression of facts to accomplish ends is opposed to newspapers' fundamental purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that arrangement and emphasis can produce constructive (preventive, wholesome) or destructive (sensational, imitative) effects. Aim for constructive treatment; avoid sensationalizing for commercial gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the story: summary lead elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The informative story usually begins with a summary lead that answers the reader's Who? What? Where? When? Why? How? — including persons, event, place, time, cause, significant circumstances. Any element may be 'featured' in lead prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft leads to include the essential elements succinctly; choose which element to feature based on news value and reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body organization and endings
rubrics_metrics.description: In the body, details follow a logical order (narrative often chronological). Only details from the lead that are needed for clearness are repeated. It's good to round out stories in the last paragraph, though makeup constraints may truncate endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange supporting facts to clarify and expand the lead; avoid unnecessary repetition and aim for a tidy, informative finish where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary style elements (paragraphs, sentences, words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style concerns paragraph and sentence length, unity of thought, coherence, and emphasis by position. Use specific words in original combinations rather than trite phrases; avoid technical words unless explained; slang/colloquial language may be used if tone justifies it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze unity and coherence in samples; prefer brisk movement and steady progress. Use humor and pathos sparingly and with taste—effective without ridicule or vulgarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style and display devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Notational choices such as abbreviation, capitalization, hyphenation, use of numerical figures, and use of boxes or bold-face for important facts vary by paper and should be applied consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note each paper's typographical conventions and follow them. Observe presentation of lists (dead/injured), market reports, and sports scores; these have standard formats to aid reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for analysis of news stories (analytic checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Points for study include: news value; sources; methods of obtaining facts; purpose of the story; type of story; structure; literary style; typographical style. Example analytic questions: In what paper was the story published? What are the policy/character of the paper? How widely does it circulate? Does it appeal to a particular class? Is the news presented from that point of view?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to dissect examples: determine why news was considered of interest, how it was obtained, what the writer/editor emphasized, and how typographical choices affect understanding.
